# Solvers

Nonlinear least squares, aimed at geometry. A constraint vocabulary — planarity, colinearity, fixed distances, perpendicularity, dihedral angles, panel areas, positions held hard or held softly — assembled into a program, compiled once and solved by Ceres across a foreign-function bridge; the architectural layer above it for gridshells and panel families; and the reuse-oriented half that re-solves the same program every frame while a user drags. Residuals you cannot express in the vocabulary can be written in Kotlin and differentiated exactly by Ceres through the expression VM. These entry points need the native Ceres library present, and nothing here draws — a solve returns points, and drawing them is your business. Start from `CeresGeometry.kt`, which is the vocabulary everything else is written in; `ArchitecturalGeometry.kt` is the layer most calls go through.

## Brief.kt { #brief-kt }

Brief is a text notation for weighted geometric constraints: points, lines, planes and panels, and
the relations they should satisfy, each with a strength.

A brief is what an architect writes before there is a building: a statement of what has to be
true, in no particular order, about things that do not exist yet. The vocabulary is the weighted
constraint set of `afield.math.optimization.ceres.ConstraintScope`, which otherwise is reachable
only from a Kotlin receiver lambda; Brief makes it available as text.

A program is a `#brief`-tagged region (a Kotlin triple-quoted string whose first line is `#brief`,
the same Route-A shape RectSL uses) or any string handed to [`compileBrief`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt--compilebrief):

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
#brief
point west  at (0, 0)
point east  at (9, 0)
fix west east

prefer spine at 1/3 along (west, east)
insist distance(west, spine) = 6
```

### Weight is a number

Every constraint statement starts with a *strength*, and the slot takes either a word from a decade
ladder ([`BriefStrength`](solvers.md#brief-kt-briefstrength)) or a bare number. `prefer` and `insist` differ by a factor of a thousand,
and the solved answer moves accordingly. The ladder words are names for numbers, so a bare number
is accepted in the same position.

### Forward reference is the normal case

Lines, planes and panels resolve in a second pass, so a relation may cite geometry declared below
it. Points are *declared on use*: naming a point that was never declared creates one, seeded on a
deterministic golden-angle circle so a brief of pure relations starts from a non-degenerate spread
rather than a pile at the origin. The invented points are listed in [`BriefProgram.inventedPoints`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt--briefprogram--inventedpoints).

### Two kinds of relation, one statement shape

`spine.length = 4` is a relation over a *property*; `spine parallel ridge` is a relation over
*elements*. Both are `strength relation`, and a relation is an equation when a top-level `=`, `>=`
or `<=` appears and a predicate otherwise. Properties and functions of elements are terms, so
`west.length = east.length` and `angle(spine, ridge) = 30deg` sit in one grammar. `planar`,
`mirrors` and `fix` have no scalar left-hand side and stay predicates. The grammar is written up in
`dev_docs/brief_notation.md`.

### Diagnostics are located and named

Every failure is a [`BriefDiagnostic`](solvers.md#brief-kt-briefdiagnostic) with a line, a column, a span and, where a name was
misspelled, a did-you-mean drawn from the names actually declared. [`compileBrief`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt--compilebrief) does not throw a
bare Kotlin exception at a program that merely reads wrong.

[`compileBrief`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt--compilebrief) is a pure function of text, with no `Box`, output or server. [`toGeometryModel`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt--togeometrymodel) turns
the result into a `GeometryModel`, and [`solve`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt--solve) solves it.

## BriefEditorExtension.kt { #briefeditorextension-kt }

The Brief editor extension's JavaScript, read from the same resource the browser loads.

The single source is the static resource `src/commonMain/resources/brief.js`, served to the browser
as the AMD module `bithero/brief` (see `bootstrapMonaco.js`) and read verbatim here, so the node
probe in `afield.examples.brief.BriefEditorExtensionWorkout` exercises the code that ships. The file
installs itself under bare `eval` and registers an AMD module when a Monaco loader is present, which
is what lets it be tested outside a browser.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/brief/BriefEditorExtension.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/brief/BriefEditorExtension/)

## BriefLowering.kt { #brieflowering-kt }

Resolution and lowering: a [`BriefSyntax`](solvers.md#brief-kt-briefsyntax) becomes a [`BriefProgram`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt-briefprogram), and a [`BriefProgram`](solvers.md#brieflowering-kt-briefprogram) becomes an
`afield.math.optimization.ceres.GeometryModel` solved through the real Ceres backend.

The two halves are separated because they fail differently. Resolution is where a *reader* is wrong
— a misspelling, a plane used where a line was wanted, two statements that cannot both hold — and
every failure there is a located [`BriefDiagnostic`](solvers.md#brief-kt-briefdiagnostic). Lowering is where the *implementation* would be
wrong, and by then every name has been checked, so it throws `error()` on anything that gets
through: an exception from this file is a bug in this file, never in the brief.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/brief/BriefLowering.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/brief/BriefLowering/)

## ArchitecturalGeometry.kt { #architecturalgeometry-kt }

A named, typed DSL over the raw constraint vocabulary in `CeresGeometry.kt`, plus the interactive
machinery for solving it while a user drags. [`geometryModel`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--geometrymodel) opens a [`GeometryModelScope`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-geometrymodelscope) where
you declare [`PointRef`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-pointref)s, [`LineRef`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-lineref)s, [`PlaneRef`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-planeref)s and [`PanelRef`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-panelref)s (points can be created from
`Vector3fc` values or bound to live `Vector3f`s via [`GeometryModelScope.bindPoint`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--geometrymodelscope--bindpoint)) and then
state relations inside `constraints { }` — [`ConstraintScope`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-constraintscope) supplies `length`, `parallelTo`,
`angleRadiansTo`, `planar`, `on`, `inside`, `lock`, `weak`, `mirror`, `dihedral` and the `ceq`
infix equality.

[`GeometryModel.openSession`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--geometrymodel--opensession) (or [`session`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--session)) compiles the program once and returns a
[`GeometrySolveSession`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-geometrysolvesession) holding a mutable point cloud, per-point prior weights and a reusable
solve report; [`GeometrySolveSession.drag`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--geometrysolvesession--drag) / [`DragHandle`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-draghandle) / `pin` / `release` are the interaction
verbs, weighted by [`InteractionPolicy`](solvers.md#interactivesolving-kt-interactionpolicy).

[`liveGeometry`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--livegeometry) wraps a model *block* rather than a model: each [`LiveGeometryProgram.step`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--livegeometryprogram--step) re-runs
the block, reuses the existing session when point names, point count and program hash are all
unchanged, reads every bound point back in, solves, and writes the results out through the
bindings. [`LiveGeometryProgram.polishLocked`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--livegeometryprogram--polishlocked) does a separate hard-locked settle pass.

Point arithmetic ([`PointExpr`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-pointexpr), `a + b`, `0.5 * c`) creates synthetic "trace" points that are
recomputed from their expression before every solve. The default backend is `FfmCeresBackend`, so
these entry points need the native Ceres library present.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/optimization/ceres/ArchitecturalGeometry.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/optimization/ceres/ArchitecturalGeometry/)

### GeometrySolveSession { #architecturalgeometry-kt-geometrysolvesession }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">GeometrySolveSession</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">model</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GeometryModel</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">backend</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">CeresSolverBackend</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">policy</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">InteractionPolicy</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AutoCloseable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/optimization/ceres/ArchitecturalGeometry/#L943)

A compiled model plus the mutable state a gesture needs: the live `points`, the per-point [`priors`](solvers.md#architecturalgeometry-kt--geometrysolvesession--priors), the reusable `report`, and the pins.

| --- | --- |

## CeresExpression.kt { #ceresexpression-kt }

Residuals written in Kotlin, compiled to a little register machine, and differentiated exactly by
Ceres.

Every other constraint in this vocabulary is a C++ functor with a matching opcode, which means a
new kind of residual costs a native rebuild, a Kotlin change, and a redeployed dylib. This is the
way out: build an expression here, [`CeresExpressionResidual`](solvers.md#ceresexpression-kt-ceresexpressionresidual) encodes it, and the native `EXPR`
opcode evaluates it. The evaluator is templated on the scalar type, so Ceres runs it on
`ceres::Jet` and gets **analytic derivatives** — not finite differences — for a residual it has
never seen.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
// "these two points are exactly 2.5 apart", written from scratch
val program = buildCeresProgram {
    expression(a, b) { (pa, pb) ->
        listOf((pa - pb).length() - 2.5.c)
    }
}
```

### What it costs

A hand-written functor is faster: the VM interprets, allocates a slot vector per evaluation, and
Ceres cannot specialise the parameter-block sizes the way [ceres::AutoDiffCostFunction] does with
a fixed arity. Reach for a real opcode when a residual is hot and settled; reach for this while
you are still finding out what the residual should be, or when it is caller-specific and will
never belong in the wrapper.

### What to watch

- [`abs`](solvers.md#ceresexpression-kt--abs), [`min`](solvers.md#ceresexpression-kt--min) and [`max`](solvers.md#ceresexpression-kt--max) are not differentiable at their kinks. Ceres will hand you a subgradient
  there, which is usually what you want for a one-sided barrier and is not what you want in the
  middle of a smooth objective.
- Nothing checks for division by zero or a square root of a negative. A residual that produces a
  NaN will make the solve fail rather than corrupt anything, but it will not tell you where.
- Ceres forbids one residual block naming the same point twice, so `expression` rejects a
  repeated point rather than letting the native side discover it.

### Sharing

The expression is a DAG, not a tree: [`CeresExpr`](solvers.md#ceresexpression-kt-ceresexpr) instances are hash-consed as you build them, so
writing `d / d` evaluates `d` once. That is why the machine is register-based — with named
destination slots, sharing is free.

### Free variables

An expression can also read *unknowns of its own* — quantities Ceres solves for that are not
points. [`CeresProgramBuilder.variable`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt--ceresprogrambuilder--variable) declares one, with an initial value and an optional
[`CeresManifold`](solvers.md#ceresexpression-kt-ceresmanifold), and hands back a [`CeresVariableRef`](solvers.md#ceresexpression-kt-ceresvariableref) that any number of expressions can name:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
// fit a sphere: the centre and the radius are unknowns, not points
val centre = variable("centre", Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
val radius = variable("radius", 1.0)
points.forEach { i ->
    expression(listOf(i), listOf(centre, radius)) { (p), (c, r) ->
        listOf(p.distanceTo(c.vec()) - r.scalar)
    }
}
```

This is the mechanism `PLANAR_HESSE` hardcodes in C++ — a plane as a unit normal on a
`SphereManifold` plus a scalar offset — made available to a residual written at runtime. It is
worth the machinery: on `kkC` the plane-as-a-free-variable formulation converges in 12 iterations
to tangency `3e-08` where the same objective with the plane eliminated inside the residual does
not converge at all. Well-conditioned auxiliary unknowns are not overhead; they are frequently
what makes a problem tractable.

The solved values come back in [`SolveResult.variables`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt--solveresult--variables), in declaration order.

## CeresGeometry.kt { #ceresgeometry-kt }

The constraint vocabulary for Field's Ceres point solver, and the encoding that ships it to a
backend. Geometry is a flat xyz [`PointCloud`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-pointcloud) addressed by [`PointId`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-pointid); a solve is described by a
[`CeresProgram`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceresprogram) of [`GeometryConstraint`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-geometryconstraint)s — [`Planar`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-planar), [`Colinear`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-colinear), [`DistanceEquals`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-distanceequals),
[`Perpendicular`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-perpendicular), [`LockPosition`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-lockposition), [`WeakPosition`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-weakposition), [`PointOnPlane`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-pointonplane), [`DihedralAngle`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-dihedralangle), [`PanelArea`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-panelarea) and
the rest — most conveniently assembled with [`buildCeresProgram`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt--buildceresprogram) / [`CeresProgramBuilder`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceresprogrambuilder).

Every constraint serialises itself into one flat `DoubleArray` of opcodes ([`CeresOpcode`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceresopcode)) via
`encodeLegacyBytecode`; the actual solving happens behind [`CeresSolverBackend`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceressolverbackend) /
[`CompiledCeresSolver`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-compiledceressolver) (see
`FfmCeresBackend.kt` for the native one). [`CachedCeresSolvers`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-cachedceressolvers) keys compiled solvers by point
count plus program hash so an unchanged program is compiled once.

Constructors validate aggressively: coordinates and weights must be finite, weights non-negative,
point indices distinct where the opcode requires it, and the `-1`/`PointId.ALL_POINTS` sentinel
may only be used alone and only where a constraint allows it.

### Weights are square-rooted, and compiling captures a pose

**Weights are square-rooted.** Every native functor stores `s = sqrt(weight)` and multiplies its
residual by `s`, so Ceres minimises `weight * residual^2`. A residual weight of `k` in the usual
"residual = k * (quantity - target)" sense is a weight of `k^2` here. Weights are also only
comparable between constraints whose residuals share units — a length, a dimensionless cosine and
an area are three different scales.

**Compiling captures a pose.** [`CeresSolverBackend.compile`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt--ceressolverbackend--compile) takes seed points, and several
constraints bake that pose in permanently: [`LockPosition`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-lockposition) pins to the seed coordinates,
[`GaugeRotation`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-gaugerotation) measures rotation relative to them, and [`Planar`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-planar) seeds each face's plane
variables from them. Points passed to a later `solve` move the answer, not those targets. The one
exception is [`WeakPosition`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-weakposition), whose target is refreshed from the input cloud on every solve — which
is what makes it a "stay near where you are" regulariser rather than a "return to the seed" one.

## InteractiveSolving.kt { #interactivesolving-kt }

The mutable, reuse-oriented half of the Ceres solver API, for solving the same program over and
over at interactive rates. [`MutablePointCloud`](solvers.md#interactivesolving-kt-mutablepointcloud), [`MutablePriorWeights`](solvers.md#interactivesolving-kt-mutablepriorweights) and [`MutableSolveReport`](solvers.md#interactivesolving-kt-mutablesolvereport)
are in-place counterparts to the immutable `PointCloud` / `DynamicPriorWeights` / `SolveMetrics`
in `CeresGeometry.kt`, so a drag loop can call [`ReusableCompiledCeresSolver.solveInPlace`](solvers.md#interactivesolving-kt--reusablecompiledceressolver--solveinplace) without
allocating a new point cloud or result per frame.

[`InteractionPolicy`](solvers.md#interactivesolving-kt-interactionpolicy) collects the weights and iteration counts that distinguish the three phases
of a drag — a cheap `dragOptions` pass while the mouse is down, a longer `releaseOptions` settle
on release, and `pinnedWeight` for points held fixed — and precomputes the matching
`SolveOptions`.
[`MutableSolveReport.top`](solvers.md#interactivesolving-kt--mutablesolvereport--top) names the highest-cost opcode groups from the last solve.

All point and weight arrays are flat xyz triples; coordinates must be finite and weights finite
and non-negative, and a report's group capacity must be at least the metric capacity a solve
asks for.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/optimization/ceres/InteractiveSolving.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/optimization/ceres/InteractiveSolving/)
